articles.title: DJ Khaled Sat Two Tables Away From Me at Sotto Sotto in Yorkville
articles.excerpt: I have been going to Sotto Sotto for almost twenty years. It is the quietest room in Yorkville. It was not quiet last Tuesday.
articles.body:
For the record, I am not someone who chases celebrities. I've lived near Avenue Road since the late nineties and Sotto Sotto has been my birthday dinner, my anniversary dinner and my "I had a terrible week" dinner more times than I can count. People always say it's where the stars eat. In twenty years I had seen exactly nobody.

So I was not prepared.

My sister and I were halfway through a bottle of Montepulciano when the host led a group of five or six past us to the back room. The man in the middle was wearing a white tracksuit, very large sunglasses and a gold chain that caught every candle in the place. Sotto Sotto is a basement. It is dim on purpose. He did not take the sunglasses off.

My sister leaned over and whispered, "That's DJ Khaled." I said, "Who?" She gave me a look I haven't received since 1994.

## The food

He was clearly very happy to be there. When the first plates came out I heard him say "this is major" quite clearly from two tables away, and then, a little later, about the tiramisu, "another one." The whole back room laughed. I gather that is one of his sayings. My sister explained it on the drive home and I'm still not sure I understand.

He filmed a few things on his phone, mostly the food, and kept holding it up and talking to it. Our server, who has been there forever, told us afterward that he asked the kitchen to come out so he could thank them on camera. They came out looking terrified and left looking delighted.

## Did anybody bother him?

Not a soul. There is an unspoken rule at Sotto Sotto about phones, and the only person who broke it was him. I found that quite funny.

He's not from here, of course, but he has worked with plenty of Toronto artists over the years, so maybe someone sent him to the right place. If you were in that room on Tuesday, tell me I didn't imagine the tracksuit.

articles.title: You Won’t Believe Who Just Sat Down Behind Me at Kost on King West
articles.excerpt: live from the Bisha rooftop. ryan gosling just walked in and everyone is suddenly very into their menus
articles.body:
ok I'm typing this under the table so ignore typos

**7:52pm.** at Kost on top of the Bisha. me and my cousin got a table by the glass because it's her birthday. whole room just went quiet for like a second. you know that thing where 40 people look at their phones at the exact same time

**7:53pm.** it's Ryan Gosling. like actually. navy jacket, white tee, ball cap pulled down. 3 people with him, look like film people. they got the corner table facing the CN Tower obviously

**8:02pm.** my cousin has watched The Notebook probably 30 times. she has not blinked in 9 minutes

**8:05pm.** he ordered a bunch of stuff for the table, tacos I think and the guac. server came back laughing at something he said so he's in a good mood I guess

**8:11pm.** couple at the bar doing the "I'm just taking a pic of my drink" angle. bro we can see you

**8:19pm.** someone near the bar said "I'm just Ken" kind of loud and the whole table looked over. he laughed. fair play

**8:30pm.** my cousin wants to go say happy birthday to HERSELF to him. I said absolutely not. she's going to the washroom "for no reason" which means walking past the table

**8:34pm.** update she walked past. he said "happy birthday" because she was wearing the birthday sash I made her wear. she is now unable to speak. this is the best birthday she's ever had and I paid for none of it

**8:58pm.** he got up, thanked the server, took one picture with her (she asked nicely, he said sure) and left through the side by the elevators

thats it. a Canadian kid from Cornwall back in Toronto eating guac on a thursday. if anyone else was up there tonight say something so I know I'm not crazy

articles.title: I Stood Behind Christina Milian in the Peameal Bacon Line at St. Lawrence Market and Had No Idea
articles.excerpt: My daughter had to explain to me who the friendly lady asking about the butter tarts was. Very nice person, for what it’s worth.
articles.body:
I'll be upfront. I didn't recognise her. My daughter did, and she made me write this.

Every second Saturday I go down to St. Lawrence Market for a peameal on a bun at Carousel Bakery. I've been doing it since before they renovated the north building. The line is always long and you just accept it.

This time the woman in front of me had on a long camel coat, big sunglasses pushed up on her head and a scarf wrapped about three times around her neck. She was with a friend and a fellow carrying a camera bag, and she kept turning around to look at all the stalls like she'd never seen a market before. At one point she asked me, very politely, if the peameal was "the thing to get." I told her it was the only thing to get. She laughed and said "okay, I trust you."

She got to the counter and ordered one with mustard, then spent a good while asking the lady about the butter tarts. How they're made, whether the filling is runny or firm, that sort of thing. She said she has a pastry business back home and she's always looking for ideas. The lady at the counter, who I've known by sight for years, gave her a little sample. They were chatting like old friends by the end.

Meanwhile there's a young woman two people behind me trying very hard not to stare and doing a very bad job of it. Eventually the lady in the coat noticed, smiled and gave her a little wave. The young woman put both hands over her mouth.

Then she took her sandwich and a box of butter tarts and went out the Front Street doors.

I got home and told my daughter about the nice American lady who wanted to know everything about butter tarts, and she grabbed my arm and said "Dad. Dad. That was Christina Milian." Apparently she's a singer and an actress and was in a lot of things my daughter watched growing up. My daughter played me one of her songs from the early two thousands. Catchy.

For the record I got my peameal and it was excellent as always. And I hope she liked the tarts.

articles.title: Was The Weeknd at Bar Raval on College Street? I Have Evidence, Not Proof
articles.excerpt: Near midnight on a Friday, someone very Weeknd-shaped slipped into the back of Bar Raval. I’ve laid out the case. You decide.
articles.body:
I'm a fourth year poli sci student, so I'm going to treat this like an essay. Bear with me.

**The setting.** Bar Raval, College Street, around 11:45 on a Friday. If you haven't been, it's the tapas bar with the wavy carved wood everywhere that looks like the inside of a cello. Packed, as always. My roommate and I were standing at the counter with sherry we couldn't really afford.

**The event.** A small group came in and went straight to the back without waiting. That alone is suspicious at Raval on a Friday.

**Evidence for:**

- Height and build were right.
- The short haircut he's had since he cut the hair off. Black bomber jacket.
- One of the guys with him looked a lot like someone I've seen in his tour photos (I checked later, I am that person).
- The bartender made a face I can only describe as "professionally calm."
- When a song off *After Hours* came on, half the room turned toward the back at once. He didn't react at all, which is either very him or very not him.

**Evidence against:**

- I never saw his face straight on. The back is dark.
- My roommate thinks I want it to be him too badly, which is fair.
- Toronto has a lot of tall guys in bomber jackets.

**What actually happened.** They shared some plates, had a couple of drinks, talked quietly for about an hour and left. Nobody went over. I'm proud of us for that.

**Conclusion.** Inconclusive. I'd say 70 percent. My roommate says 40. If you were at Raval that night and got a better look, please settle this, because we have been arguing about it for three days.
articles.faq:

A: Unconfirmed. The writer never saw the person's face clearly and puts the odds at about 70 percent.
Q: Where is Bar Raval?
A: Bar Raval is a Spanish style tapas bar at 505 College Street, on the edge of Toronto's Little Italy.

A: Yes. The Weeknd (Abel Tesfaye) was born and raised in Toronto, in the Scarborough area.

articles.title: Will Smith Held the Door for Me at the Distillery District and I Walked Into a Sign
articles.excerpt: Six seconds with Will Smith at Balzac’s. I spent five of them making noises that weren’t words.
articles.body:
I want it on the record that I am a functioning adult. I have a job. I pay a mortgage on a condo the size of a parking spot. I can talk to people.

Not this day, though.

Sunday afternoon, I'm doing the Distillery District thing with my girlfriend. Cobblestones, overpriced candles, the guy with the roasted almonds. We go to get coffee at Balzac's in the old brick pump house and the door is heavy, and a hand reaches over my shoulder and holds it.

I turn to say thanks. It's Will Smith.

Here is the full conversation, word for word:

Him: "Go ahead, man."

Me: "Th. Ye. Thank. Thanks."

Him: *big grin*

Me: *walks directly into the A-frame menu sign*

He actually laughed and said "you good?" and I said "yep" in a voice about an octave higher than my normal one. My girlfriend has told this story to eleven people so far. I've counted.

Anyway. Once I could see straight again I noticed he was with a couple of people who looked like they were working. One had a binder with tabs and kept pointing up at the brick buildings. The Distillery gets used for film shoots all the time so I'm guessing they were scouting. He had a ball cap and a black puffer on and honestly looked like he was freezing. It was nine degrees.

He ordered a hot chocolate, which I respect, and got talking basketball with the barista. The barista said the Raptors would beat Philly this year. He laughed and said "we'll see about that" and then shook the guy's hand on the way out like they'd made a bet. Then he wandered off toward Trinity Street.

So if you were at Balzac's and saw a grown man in a Raptors toque fall into a sign in front of the Fresh Prince, hello. That was me. I'm fine.

articles.title: I Said “Hej” to Alexander Skarsgård in the Line at Pai and He Answered in Swedish
articles.excerpt: I am a homesick Swedish student in Toronto. The very tall man ducking under the stairs at Pai Northern Thai Kitchen made my whole month.
articles.body:
I moved to Toronto from Gothenburg last year to do my master's at U of T. I like it here very much, but some weeks I miss home a lot. This was one of those weeks, so my friend Maya took me to Pai on Duncan Street, because she says nobody can be sad while eating Thai food.

If you have been to Pai, you know the entrance. You go down a narrow staircase into the basement and the ceiling is quite low. While we were waiting on the stairs, a man in front of us had to bend his head forward the whole time, because he was so tall. Long grey wool coat, a black beanie, a little bit of beard.

He turned around to say something to his friend and I knew the face immediately. In Sweden everybody knows the Skarsgård family. It was Alexander Skarsgård.

## The moment

I did something I have never done before. I said, very quietly, "hej."

He looked down at me (very far down) and smiled and said "hej hej! Är du svensk?" Are you Swedish? I said yes, from Gothenburg, and he said he is from Stockholm but "we can still be friends." We talked for maybe one minute in Swedish about how Toronto winter is not so bad compared to home, and how Canadians apologise even more than Swedes do. Then the host called his name and he said "ha det bra," which is like "take care."

Maya does not speak Swedish. She just stared at me the whole time with her mouth open.

## What he ate

They sat two tables away. I tried not to look but I am human. He ordered the gaeng hung lay, the pork belly curry, and asked the server to make it "mild, I'm Scandinavian." Later he asked for a little more chili on the side and I respected that very much. His friend had the khao soi. They shared mango sticky rice at the end.

When he left he waved to our table and said "hej då." Maya says this was the best dinner I have had since I moved here. She is correct.

I know Succession fans in Toronto will ask: no, he was not wearing a vest. Just a sweater. Very normal.

articles.title: Angelina Jolie Asked for a Nina Simone Record at Vinny on King West and the Whole Room Went Quiet
articles.excerpt: I go to Vinny for the records, not the people. Then a woman from one of the back tables walked up to the DJ and asked for side B of a Nina Simone album.
articles.body:
Quick context. I've been collecting records since I was fourteen and I spin at a couple of small nights around the city. When Vinny opened on King West in the old Pink Sky spot, I was there the first week. A proper listening bar, records on the wall, a real sound system, low lights, people actually paying attention to the music. It's my happy place.

I go for the records. I do not go for the people. So I wasn't looking around much on Saturday night.

My buddy Marcus and I were at the bar around 10:30. The selector was deep into a run of seventies soul and I was trying to guess every track before the needle dropped. I was losing.

Then a woman got up from one of the booths near the back and walked over to the DJ booth. Dark hair pulled back, black turtleneck, no jewelry I could see. She leaned in and said something, and the selector's eyebrows went all the way up.

Marcus grabbed my arm. "Bro. Bro. That's Angelina Jolie."

## The request

I heard it, because she wasn't trying to be loud but the room is built for sound. She asked if they had any Nina Simone, and if so, could they play something off side B. Not the hits. Side B.

That is a correct request. That is a record person request.

The selector dug for about a minute, found it, and dropped the needle. The whole room kind of went quiet. Not because of her, I think, but because it was a beautiful record on a beautiful system and everybody felt it at the same time. She stood by the booth for the whole first song with her eyes closed, then said thank you and went back to her table.

## The rest of the night

She was with three or four people who looked like they worked in film. It's festival season, so King West is full of that. Nobody went over to her table. Somebody near the windows tried a sneaky photo and a bartender very politely asked him to put the phone away. Good on Vinny.

She left around midnight. On the way out she stopped at the booth again and said something to the selector that made him laugh.

I asked him later what she said. He told me she said "good pressing." I've been thinking about it for three days.

articles.title: Oscar Isaac Was at the Next Table at Kiin on Our Anniversary, and My Mom Will Never Believe Me
articles.excerpt: Ten years married, one fancy Thai dinner on Adelaide, and a very familiar face two tables over. Then I heard him speaking Spanish.
articles.body:
My husband Rob and I don't do fancy dinners very often. We have two kids, a dog and a mortgage in Etobicoke. But it was our tenth anniversary, so I booked Kiin on Adelaide months ahead. It's the royal Thai place from the same people who do Pai, and everyone says it's a special occasion restaurant. It is. The room is calm and warm and beautiful and every plate comes out looking like art.

We were maybe twenty minutes in, working on these little bites that came on a carved wooden tray, when Rob put his fork down and said, very quietly, "Don't look now. Poe Dameron."

I looked now. Obviously.

Two tables over, a man in a dark green sweater, curly hair, a short beard, laughing with two friends. Oscar Isaac. I have seen Dune maybe four times. I know that face.

## Then it got personal

My parents came to Toronto from Guatemala before I was born. Oscar Isaac was born in Guatemala too, which my mom has told me roughly a thousand times. So when I heard him switch into Spanish with one of his friends, I kind of melted.

On our way to the washroom, I passed his table. I didn't plan to say anything, but it came out anyway: "Perdón, solo quería decir que mi familia es de Guatemala también." Sorry, I just wanted to say my family is from Guatemala too.

He lit up. Asked which city. I said Quetzaltenango, he said "¡Qué bonito!" and asked if I'd been back recently. We talked for maybe thirty seconds. He was so warm about it. Then I said "buen provecho" and left him to his dinner, because I am not a monster.

## The food, for the record

This is not Pai. It's slower and fancier, the kind of meal where the server explains every dish and you actually want to listen. There was a curry I will be thinking about for a year. Rob had a fish dish he described as "life changing," and he describes nothing that way.

I've heard people say there's a lot of filming happening in Toronto lately, so maybe that explains it. Or maybe he just likes good Thai food. Either way, I called my mom from the car. She asked if I got a photo. I did not. She says it didn't happen.

It happened, Mom.

articles.title: Stephen Curry Was Eating Late Night Tacos at Silent H on King West After the Game
articles.excerpt: Raptors lost, my rec league buddies and I went for tacos to drown our sorrows, and the guy who just beat us walked in.
articles.body:
Let me set the scene. Four grown men who play Tuesday night rec league at a church gym in Leslieville. All lifelong Raptors fans. All in the 300 level at Scotiabank Arena watching the Warriors do the thing the Warriors always do to us.

We lose. We're sad. Somebody says tacos. We walk over to Silent H on King because it's open till 2 and the margaritas are strong.

Around 11:30, we've got a table full of tacos and guac and we're breaking down everything that went wrong in the fourth quarter like we're on TSN. Then the door opens and three or four guys come in, and the first one is wearing a black hoodie and a Warriors cap.

My buddy Dre stops mid sentence. Just freezes, holding a taco.

It's Steph Curry. The same Steph Curry who hit about four threes on us in the third quarter. Walking into the taco place we picked to get over it.

## The most Toronto thing ever

Here's what a lot of people forget. Steph actually lived here as a kid, when his dad Dell played for the Raptors. He went to school in Etobicoke for a year. So when the server asked if it was his first time in Toronto, he laughed and said "nah, I'm basically a local," and the whole bar kind of cheered.

They sat at a table by the back. He ordered what looked like a big spread of tacos for the group and a lot of chips. He was relaxed, laughing, looking at his phone with his teammates. Normal guys eating dinner after work. Their work just happens to be beating my team.

## Did we talk to him?

Dre wanted to. I said we'd lost enough tonight already. But on the way out, Steph walked past our table, saw Dre's vintage Vince Carter jersey and said "respect, that's a classic." Dre has not taken that jersey off since.

I came for tacos to forget about the game. Instead I'll remember it forever. Still mad about the third quarter though.

articles.title: Benny Blanco Got So Excited About a Steak at Prime Seafood Palace That He Stood Up
articles.excerpt: I’m a culinary student. I saved for two months to eat at Prime Seafood Palace on Queen West. The most entertaining thing on the menu turned out to be the guy at the next table.
articles.body:
I'm in my second year of culinary school at George Brown and I work weekends at a bakery in the Junction. Dinners like Prime Seafood Palace are not a normal thing for me. I put away a little from every paycheque for two months to take my roommate there for her birthday, and I planned to pay attention to every single plate.

I did. But I also paid a lot of attention to table six.

The room is all warm wood and soft light, the kind of place where everyone talks a little quieter than usual. So you notice when someone at the next table goes "oh my GOD" at full volume after the first bite of bread.

I looked over. Curly hair, round glasses, an oversized striped shirt, a huge smile. My roommate kicked me under the table and mouthed "Benny Blanco." The music producer. The guy who is always posting videos of himself eating things and losing his mind about them. He was doing exactly that, except in real life, two metres from me.

## The steak moment

When their steak came out, he actually stood up. Not to leave. Just to look at it from above, the way you'd look at a painting. He asked the server a bunch of questions about how long it was aged and what kind of wood they cook over, and he listened to every answer like he was going to be tested on it. As a culinary student, I respected this deeply.

Then he cut a piece, closed his eyes, and did a little seated dance. His friends were dying laughing. So was half the room.

## Was he nice?

Very. When our server came back to our table, she told us he'd asked to send his compliments to the kitchen "and also to whoever made the bread, specifically, I need them to know." Later, on his way out, he passed our table, saw the little birthday candle in my roommate's dessert and said "happy birthday! Did you get the bread? You have to get the bread."

We had gotten the bread. He was right about the bread.

My chef instructors are always telling us that people remember how food made them feel. I don't think I've ever seen someone feel more about a steak.

articles.title: My Aunty Told Joe Jonas What to Order at Adrak Yorkville, and He Listened
articles.excerpt: I took my mom and two aunties for a fancy Indian dinner on Avenue Road. They had no idea who the polite young man at the next table was. I did.
articles.body:
Some context about my family. My mom and her sisters grew up in Delhi, raised us in Brampton, and believe that no restaurant Indian food will ever be as good as theirs. So when I got my first real bonus at work, I booked Adrak on Avenue Road to prove them wrong. Fancy room, low lights, beautiful plates. Mom put on her good earrings. Big night.

We'd barely sat down when Pinky Aunty leaned over and whispered, very loudly, as aunties do: "That boy is so handsome. Is he an actor?"

I turned around. Navy blazer, white t-shirt, that perfect hair. Joe Jonas. Of the Jonas Brothers. Of DNCE. Of every poster on my bedroom wall in 2008.

I said "Aunty, he's a singer." She said "From where?" I said "America." She said "Hm. Okay," and went back to her menu. My mom didn't look up at all.

## Then Pinky Aunty got involved

Joe and his two friends were clearly debating the menu. I heard one of them say "let's just get the butter chicken," and before I could stop her, Pinky Aunty turned all the way around in her chair and said "Beta, no. You can get butter chicken anywhere. Get the lamb. And the dal. Trust me."

I wanted to die. I truly wanted to leave my body.

But Joe just laughed, put his hand on his heart, and said "Yes ma'am. Lamb and dal. Thank you." And when the server came, he ordered exactly that. He even pointed over at our table and said "she told me to."

## The review, from the aunties

At the end of the night he stopped by our table on his way out and told Pinky Aunty she was right, the lamb was the best thing he'd eaten all week. She looked very satisfied. Then he said "have a great night, ladies" and left.

In the car, my mom finally spoke. "Very good manners, that boy." From her, that's basically a Grammy.

And for the record, they admitted the food was almost as good as home. Almost.

articles.title: Russell Crowe Picked His Fish Off the Ice at Estiatorio Milos, Then Talked Rugby With My Client
articles.excerpt: A routine client dinner on Bay Street. My client is from Sydney. The man choosing a sea bream at the fish display was Russell Crowe. You can guess how the rest of the night went.
articles.body:
I work in finance, two blocks from Milos, and I take clients there more often than my expense report would like. It's a reliable room. White walls, bright light, and that long display of fresh fish laid out on ice near the entrance on Adelaide, where you walk up and choose what you want grilled. Clients love the theatre of it. I usually let them pick.

On Thursday my guest was a portfolio manager from Sydney, in town for three days of meetings. Pleasant, sharp, extremely passionate about rugby league. I had prepared for a conversation about rates. I was not prepared for what happened.

We were standing at the fish display while the server walked us through the options. Next to us, a broad man with a grey beard, a flat cap and a heavy wool coat was doing the same thing, leaning in close and asking very specific questions about a sea bream. He had an accent my client recognised before I did.

My client turned to me and said, under his breath, "Mate. That's Russell Crowe."

## The rugby portion of the evening

I would like to say my client played it cool. He did not. He waited until Crowe had chosen his fish, then said "Sorry to bother you. Big Rabbitohs fan." Crowe is famously tied to the South Sydney Rabbitohs and helped buy the club years ago, I learned later.

Crowe's whole face changed. He shook my client's hand and the two of them stood beside the ice for a solid five minutes, discussing a season I know nothing about, in an accent that got thicker by the sentence. I nodded at what I hoped were the right moments.

Then he said "enjoy the fish, it's the best in town," and went back to his table near the window with a small group.

## Business outcome

For the record, the dinner was excellent. The grilled octopus was perfect, the fish was simple and very fresh, and the bill was what you'd expect for Bay Street. My client stopped by Crowe's table on our way out to say goodnight. Crowe raised his glass and said "Go Souths."

We signed the deal the next week. I'm not saying the two things are related. My client is.

articles.title: I Recognised Davis Schneider by the Moustache at Jacobs & Co. Steakhouse and Got My Napkin Signed
articles.excerpt: I’ve been a Blue Jays fan since 1992. My husband took me to Jacobs for our anniversary, and the young man at the bar had a very famous moustache.
articles.body:
I want to start by saying I have been a Blue Jays fan since Joe Carter. I was at the SkyDome (I will never call it anything else) in '92 and '93 and I have had season tickets in the 500 level for longer than some of the current players have been alive. So I know my Jays.

Last Friday was our 35th anniversary. My husband Gary, who has never once booked a restaurant in our entire marriage, surprised me with a reservation at Jacobs & Co. on Brant Street. Very fancy. Dark wood, white tablecloths, steak knives that look like they could do surgery. Gary wore a tie. I nearly fainted before we even got to the celebrity part.

We were early, so we sat at the bar first. Three seats down there was a young fellow in a navy quarter zip with a couple of friends, laughing about something on his phone. I couldn't see his face properly. But when he turned around, there it was.

The moustache.

I grabbed Gary's arm so hard he spilled his martini. "Gary. GARY. That's Davis Schneider."

Gary said "Who?" Thirty five years, people. Thirty five years and he still doesn't know the roster.

## I behaved, mostly

It had only been a few days since the news that the Jays weren’t bringing him back, so I figured the poor man just wanted a quiet dinner with his friends. I waited. I waited a full ten minutes, which for me is a personal record. Then, when his friends went to the washroom, I leaned over and said "I'm so sorry, I don't want to bother you. I just want to say we’re really going to miss you at the dome."

He could not have been nicer. Big smile, said "that means a lot, thank you," and asked how long I'd been going to games. When I said since '92 he said "so you've seen it all." I said "I've seen enough." He laughed at that, and said Toronto would always be a special place for him.

I didn't have anything for him to sign, so I handed him a cocktail napkin. He signed it and drew a little moustache next to his name. A little moustache! I'm having it framed.

## The steak

Oh, and the dinner. I had the filet, Gary had something dry aged that he wouldn't stop talking about, and we split a Caesar salad that I'm still thinking about. Best anniversary I've had. Sorry Gary, it wasn't the steak.

articles.title: Michael Timmins May Have Been Talking City Winery at Gusto 501
articles.excerpt: I went for pasta in Corktown and left convinced I had spotted a Cowboy Junkie quietly workshopping Toronto’s next dinner-and-a-show room.
articles.body:
I am not normally the person who recognizes musicians in restaurants. I once failed to notice a Leafs player standing directly beside me because I was comparing focaccia prices on my phone. So please understand the humility involved when I say this: I think I saw Michael Timmins from Cowboy Junkies at Gusto 501 on Sunday night.

This was November 22, three days after I read that City Winery was officially coming to Toronto. My cousin and I were at Gusto 501 because I had spent the afternoon helping her build a bed frame in Corktown, by which I mean I held one Allen key and said things like, “Maybe flip it?” Dinner was my emotional compensation.

Gusto 501 is the tall, terracotta-glowing Italian place at 501 King Street East, the one that looks like someone stacked several stylish dinner parties on top of each other. It is all warm clay walls, glass, stairs, and people trying not to look impressed by the room. I failed immediately. I looked impressed by the room.

## The table that seemed a little too musical

We were seated partway up, close enough to see the movement between levels but not close enough to pretend I understood the architecture. Our server was very patient with us, especially when my cousin asked what “panelle” was and I whispered, “Italian pancake?” with the confidence of a man who has never been right about anything.

A few tables over, there was a small group, maybe four people. Nothing flashy. No big security energy. No one doing the performative sunglasses indoors routine. Just a calm table with menus, wine glasses, and that quiet seriousness people get when they are discussing something more important than whether to order the mafalde ai funghi.

Then I noticed one guy in a dark jacket, greyish hair, glasses, very low-key. He looked familiar in that Toronto way, where you cannot tell if someone is a respected musician or the parent of someone you went to high school with. I kept glancing over, not in a creepy way, more in a “my brain is buffering” way.

And then it clicked. Michael Timmins. Guitarist, songwriter, founding member of Cowboy Junkies. The band formed in Toronto in the 1980s, and their whole thing has always felt like the city after midnight, quiet, a little haunted, very good at making you stare out a window.

## Why City Winery was already in my head

The only reason I connected the dots so fast is because I had just read about City Winery Toronto. The New York-born music, wine, and dining concept is supposed to open its first Canadian location at ROQ City, the big mixed-use development at 261 Queen Street East. That is not far from Gusto 501, especially if you are the kind of person who has already walked too much and starts describing everything east of Church as “basically nearby.”

The announcement said the Toronto outpost is expected in early 2028 and will be at ROQ City in the St. Lawrence area. It is meant to be a seated listening room with dinner, a full restaurant and bar, private event spaces, Canadian wine, and programming that mixes local artists with touring acts. ROQ City itself has been described as music-inspired, with residential towers, retail space, and a public park planned into the project.

The Cowboy Junkies connection was also fresh. Michael Timmins had been quoted praising City Winery’s intimate listening-room setup after the band’s recent run at City Winery in New York. So when a man who looked a lot like him was sitting at Gusto 501, not far from the future Toronto site, talking quietly with a few people while the rest of us were attacking pizza, my little gossip brain started doing cartwheels.

Was he there because of City Winery? I have no proof. Was he eating dinner like a normal person who deserves privacy and bread? Absolutely. But the timing was suspiciously neat, and I am weak.

## Pasta, wine, and one very polite possible rock legend

Our table ordered focaccia, arancini, the mafalde ai funghi, and a margherita pizza because my cousin believes balance means “one mushroom thing, one cheese thing.” Gusto’s menu is very good for this kind of evening, Italian but not sleepy, with pastas, pizzas, grilled things, desserts, and the famous house vino poured by the ounce. I did not order the $1-an-ounce vino because I had work the next morning, which is the kind of sentence that makes me feel 900 years old.

The possible Michael Timmins table seemed relaxed. I am not going to pretend I heard every word, because I did not, and also the room has a healthy buzz to it. But I did catch phrases that sounded like “room,” “audience,” and “Toronto,” which could mean a new music venue or could mean literally any conversation in this city between October and April.

What stood out was how unshowy the whole thing felt. He listened more than he talked, nodded at the server, and at one point moved a glass so plates could be set down more easily. I have decided this is the true celebrity test. Not autographs. Not dramatic entrances. Just whether you make space for the person carrying hot food.

My cousin, who is less sentimental than me and once described a famous actor as “that tall sleep-deprived man,” agreed that it looked like him. She then told me not to say anything because “Toronto only works if everyone pretends not to notice.” Correct, unfortunately.

So I said nothing. I ate my pasta. I looked at the terracotta walls like they might confirm things for me. They did not.

## What I can actually swear to

I can swear I was at Gusto 501 in Corktown on Sunday night, November 22. I can swear I saw a man who looked very much like Michael Timmins of Cowboy Junkies sitting with a few people at a nearby table. I can swear he seemed friendly, quiet, and completely uninterested in being a spectacle.

I cannot swear it was him. I did not ask. I did not take a photo. I did not hover by the stairs pretending to check my email, although I considered it and rejected it because I still have a shred of dignity.

But with the City Winery Toronto announcement landing that same week, and the future venue being just up around Queen East, I am filing this under “unverified but deliciously plausible.” Rumour only. Pasta confirmed.
